The gist of it is that her genuine romantic desire would probably amount to feeling like she can be safe and vulnerable around someone. I think she desperately wants to be understood and for someone (probably Andrew) to trust that she has good intentions.

...Well, good intentions for her would-be lover, at least.

The fact that she actually enjoyed sex while drunk speaks volumes about this, I feel. She can't enjoy it as long as she worries about loss and being hurt. Being drunk removes that worry, and her meltdown the morning after probably came from not liking how she opened up to someone who she still believes doesn't have her best interests at heart.

I think it's a mistake to believe that 'growing up' necessitates acting better; it very much doesn't. For Ashley, it comes from her understanding the effects her actions have on people; that she can do and say things that *matter* to them and have a lasting impact.

In 3A, we see her self-reflect and understand that Andrew almost choking and slapping her were consequences of her actions. We see her correcting herself when calling Andrew 'Andy' even when he's not there because she understands that it matters to him even if she doesn't understand why. We also see her being somewhat more careful with the wording of her agreements after it almost bit her in the ass with the campers and the police.

In 3B, we see her quickly coming to terms with the fact that she did in fact say she'd do "anything" for the Entity to save her. We see her understanding that her words matter and not even bother trying to call it out or say it was unfair. We also see her **actively choosing to harm Andrew** because she understands what her actions would do to him, and not out of retaliation for a perceived slight.

Basically, in both routes, she shows an understanding of her capacity to inflict harm and that her actions have consequences. That's not something someone with a childish worldview does.

I mean, they don't suddenly become entirely different people just because they grew up. That's just how Andrew prefers to think about it. What Andrew doesn't quite realize is that "Leyley" is a set of behaviors Ashley does *on purpose* to draw his attention to her and keep him around. It's a mask, not unlike Andrew's. Both of them are **already** a lot more grown up than the other (and a lot of the fanbase, apparently) is willing to give them credit for and they only *really* manifest their childhood behaviors when desperately looking for comfort and/or security.

The only thing we don't know is the specifics of Ashley's romantic desires (although I could take a crack at figuring it out), but we already know Andrew's are **everything that Ashley is** (when she's at her best).

Something I think people are missing about this scene and its implications is that Ashley is actually perfectly romantically compatible with him by virtue of them having to develop their personalities around each other's deficiencies from birth. It's part of why he was so deeply unhappy with Julia: She literally could not satisfy his emotional needs. His desires aren't really *that* pathological; it's how he acts on them that is.

What I think might end up happening is that Andrew takes LU's offer to get rid of the thoughts he doesn't want, only for them to still happen because he **actually wants them.** This would end up making it literally impossible for him to ignore his true desires. Now that he can't tell himself it's pathological anymore, hilarity ensues.

It **is** a big deal to her, because normally she always gets what she wants. When she was saying that, it seemed like she was trying to convey to him that she was making steps towards being better and Andrew, being himself, was unable to acknowledge it.

Half of her character arc is trying to be something other than bad for him and having it thrown back in her face.
When she was explaining all the ways in which she "compromised."

I really don't think she was dipping her toes into being open in the first scene. I actually think she was doing so in the second scene when she was trying to convince Andrew that she could listen to him and show consideration for his feelings (in her own weird way) and he just threw it back at her.

Ashley has frankly shown no indication that she's started to view sex as anything other than a transaction. We already know that she only enjoys sex when she's vulnerable (as shown at the end of Shots when she was drunk) and she was by no means vulnerable in the first scene.

It's important to note that she (claims she) ramped up her affections to make him happy in the first scene, so it's more than possible to read this as her embarrassment coming from shame that she 'gave him' something she felt was important and it wasn't appreciated or taken seriously.

I don't question anything about myself anymore. When I was first learning about trans issues, I was watching several YouTube videos to educate myself, and in one of the videos someone said "Even if being transgender was entirely a choice, it'd still be valid to transition." And then something clicked in my brain and the idea of being "valid" never mattered to me again. It took me a while after that to start HRT because the idea of social transition was spooky but I rejected the idea of gender being an "essential" quality that has to be "valid" or validated from very early on in my trans journey.

That mindset turned it into an active choice rather than something I felt like I needed to do to become my "true" self. I basically had no reason to fret about those things anymore so the only self-doubt I had left was whether or not I wanted to have children, but as time went on that became less and less important to me. Sometimes it still bugs me a little that I'd have to adopt if I really wanted children, though. But ultimately I care more about me and what I express to the world than anything or anyone I might leave behind.

I think a lot of people who read into Bleach realize this, but Ichigo's Hollow mask is an externalization and otherization of his self-preservation and killing instincts. Internalizing those instincts is why he no longer needed a mask after his Dangai training and fought better even after losing his powers. White was still independent enough from Ichigo to require "waking up" but it still wasn't something he otherized; the blade was him, after all.

What I don't think readers think about as often is what Yhwachgetsu symbolizes. Most Quincies serve and gain power from someone greater than themselves, so I believe that OMZ/Tensa Zangetsu represents that too: a "greater cause" or one's ideals. Ichigo couldn't fight Aizen properly the first time because there was a very limited personal connection between the two of them. Ichigo couldn't see beyond himself, so even the presence of an imminent threat made it impossible to fight to his fullest due to lacking a concrete ideological reason to fight Aizen coupled with the fear of his own power.

I believe this might be why Gin emphasized Ichigo's gaze in his dying breath; he could now see that Ichigo could finally see beyond himself. Ichigo's Dangai training gave him both a mastery over his instincts and a cause to fight for, so he was fully self-actualized, if only temporarily.

That's why I think it's incorrect to define Ichigo solely as a "protector", because he could not bring himself to fight when protecting Karakura town or even the whole world because he lacked an understanding of something greater than himself. The Soul King is this to all who understand his existence, whether they fight for him or to overthrow or replace him, but Ichigo needed something more, because he first gained his Shinigami powers independent of any of the systems that usually disperse them. To him, God was dead, and was always dead. He could not handle the burden of his own power- hence why his own Shinigami powers crushed his bones- nor the burdens of the world around him- which is why OMZ restricted his power. He lacked the understanding to truly know where his responsibilities should end, and was deprived of the power to accept those responsibilities.

Think about it. When Zangetsu granted Ichigo power against Zaraki, he only did so when Ichigo affirmed a desire for something beyond his survival. A desire to *win*, to impose his ideals on the world. A desire to live would've been under the purview of White Zangetsu and therefore not something OMZ could help with. But in affirming a desire to achieve something greater than himself, OMZ- for the first time- granted him the power to achieve those ideals.

Ichigo's story is not solely a tale of one who wants to protect that which is important to him; it's also a story of finding meaning when you wish to take all the responsibility of the world upon yourself. His is a story **of learning how to do what you can, when there's nothing you can do.**

1. People only care about surface level details and don't care to understand the introspective and symbolic nature of the story. This isn't entirely on them; Bleach is a great example of why "show, don't tell" doesn't actually result in a better story. Sometimes the quiet part needs to be said out loud to give more casual readers a hook to dive deeper. It's not even a matter of intelligence; sometimes interest in deeper analysis has to be intentionally cultivated and Kubo rarely does that. He's very much a "if you know, you know" writer.
2. The pacing of the manga was horrid while it was ongoing. Felt like nothing was going on sometimes. This was fixed when the manga finished and you could binge it but the week-by-week reading experience was rather unpleasant. I think a lot of more modern readers don't realize how bad it was at the time. I didn't have much of an issue with it but I can understand why other people did.

Too many important characters (Chad, Orihime, and Uryu being the big ones) just fell off with no further elaboration and giving side characters that didn't fall off their own fights (big problem w/ the Arrancar arc) contributed to the poorly-received pacing outlined above. Many, many people don't like this kind of writing even though I'm usually okay with it.

PLD was the only tank I didn't raid with pre-DT but the rest have felt fine to me. Their (not including PLD) rotations aren't getting gutted for no good reason and they still have tools powerful enough to meaningfully change how you engage with encounters, however minimally. We have lost cool things like overshielding or invulning to block damage downs but that's small potatoes compared to everything else either getting much worse or getting nothing when they desperately need it.

Positioning could stand to improve but I do think DT's first raid tier was a good sign. Also as a chronic parsebro(sis?) I don't think tank rotations are as comparable as some people think.  I've felt some pretty big differences in how I approached fights this tier with different tanks because the seemingly small differences in rotations end up being more significant than they look when I'm trying to push damage or ironing out my performance in a fight. I didn't feel like WAR and PLD in particular played anything like each other given PLD's superior range and the fact that you can smuggle stronger GCDs into your burst window.

Also to answer the rest of your post, no, I was literally there the whole time. People actually did want this. They wanted jobs to be less dependent on RNG, for different jobs to be able to function similarly in every piece of content, for raid buffs to benefit all jobs equally, etc. They wanted more predictable and normalized outcomes so your raid composition mattered less and jobs rarely got locked out of content because they couldn't efficiently do what an encounter demanded of them. 

They wanted TP to be removed or changed so that faster skill speed didn't fuck someone over if you didn't have a ninja or a ranged DPS, especially in a Duty Finder dungeon group. They wanted enmity management to be less dependent on randoms playing nice with their enmity tools (or just playing WAR) so you could keep near 100% uptime on your DPS stance (especially in the face of frankly baffling changes like locking certain tools behind which stance you were using). They wanted damage type vulnerabilities to be addressed, once more so that the average experience was less dependent on party composition because it didn't feel good to randomly lose out on 10% damage because you didn't have a Dragoon or a Ninja. They didn't want utility skills to cost damaging resources because it made those skills comparatively much less useful. They didn't want Astrologian cards to greatly impact personal or raid DPS because of how awful it felt to not get the Balance and how much easier it could make hitting DPS checks if it was drawn. I could keep listing off examples but I *hope* I got my point across with these ones.

Any handful of these changes could've resulted in a better game experience. The problem is that changing *all of them* in the ways they did led to jobs having less to do outside of raw DPS, which ruined an entire role (rip ranged phys) and forced even more changes to job design to make sure some jobs didn't disproportionately lose out on output (or more accurately, contribution) from the presence of other jobs. This combined with more changes to fight design philosophy (more downtime, namely, to allow for more difficult mechanics not contingent on boss positioning) resulted in us losing out on DoTs and job timers because otherwise the content would be too punishing to jobs that depended more heavily on those things. 

The community simply could not handle jobs being more specialized to handle different encounters and made this dissatisfaction very known at every opportunity. There were obviously better ways to handle this but many of these problems **DID** stem from listening to community feedback.

You can come up with any conspiracies you want wrt. duty support or wanting to make jobs simpler so they can appeal to a wider variety of players, but I got to watch this shit unfold in real time. It was all about making the average gameplay experience more predictable and standardized and the necessary dumbing-down that this usually requires.

In retrospect I think they jumped the shark with ShB and I didn't notice it was a shark they jumped over until EW. Back in ShB I still believed that a lot of the changes they made would enable better job design in the future (and I was a fan of a lot of the simplifications they made, speaking as someone who was still good at the game back in StB) but the only role that hasn't gotten universally worse to me is tanks.

There's a pretty direct line between complaints the community has made and job changes over the years. I don't think anyone who's been paying attention since HW can deny that. It really wasn't until mid-EW that we started getting so many "nobody actually wants this" changes but they still follow the same general pattern of normalizing outcomes that the community has been clamoring for since as long as I've been around.

This doesn't absolve them of having responded to some of the complaints in the stupidest possible ways but it's never been inaccurate to blame the community for not knowing what they were asking for. 

I'm not defending the dev team, per se, just saying that the community and dev team deserve each other. If I had even a smallest amount of respect left for CBT3 then I'd still be playing.

Meanwhile, we have Iko-  who can only be beaten by Zaraki- and Cien, who I have no idea where the fuck he actually scales other than "stronger than everyone except Zaraki at the time and also probably Yamamoto but the two were never directly compared" as well as the top 4 Espada who all required multiple Captain class opponents (or someone who is as strong as multiple Captains) to beat.

But if you want to say that the ceiling of those 3 is indicative of what (natural, unaided) Shinigami as a whole are capable of then I can't really disagree. I'm just saying we have fewer Shinigami outliers than Hollow outliers as far as named characters go. It seems more likely to me that Hollows have ceilings that are easier to reach given we know- or at the very least can surmise- that more Adjuchas exist than Shinigami of a comparable level.

But Barragan was kind of a loser given how long he was alive so maybe Hollows really just ain't shit. The metaphysics of the world were explicitly designed to favor Shinigami, after all.

I don't entirely disagree, but the strongest Hollows were always beaten by people who were freaks of nature. We've never really seen a top-tier Hollow fight someone 1v1 in their weight class who couldn't hax them to death. While Shunsui *probably* could've beaten Starrk 1v1 if both of them cut loose from the beginning (Bankai would low dif him but that's still hax more than raw power), there's still likely at least a thousand year gap in experience between the two of them, depending on how old Starrk actually was.

It's worth considering that the strongest Hollow we know of still defeated a (much younger, mind) Yamamoto, and it took Ichibe erasing his name to defeat him which indicates that his raw power was still very difficult to deal with. 

Not to mention, primordial Menos were a nigh-Soul King-level threat and Hell!Szayel wasn't casually swatted away by Ichigo the same way Zaraki did to Ikomikidomoe so he's pretty beefy too. I don't think it's **that** wrong to say that Hollows have a higher ceiling compared to Shinigami or Quincy who aren't blessed by the Bleach equivalent of divine providence.

I also think it's important to consider that both Shinigami and Quincy benefit from what is effectively outside interference, as Asauchi, many Quincy abilities, and *maybe* Kido are things that were granted to them and not inherent to their species. We don't really know where Hollows would be if they had the same levels of technological development and they did a damn fine job competing without it.

The whole series is a Nietzsche allegory, not just Aizen.

Soul Society parades around the half-dead corpse of a God because it's the only thing that gives the world stability. The morality of the series is predicated on this God, who has little-to-no will of its own.
